newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: China seen allowing U.N. peace mission to Guatemala.
newsitem.headline: China seen allowing U.N. peace mission to Guatemala.

text.p: Guatemala said on Thursday it was confident China would not block a U.N. peacekeeping mission here after Guatemalan and Chinese envoys met in New York to address their differences over Taiwan.

China, rankled over Guatemala's close ties with Taiwan, had withheld support for a U.N. Security Council resolution to send 155 U.N. peacekeepers to monitor the end of Guatemala's 36-year-old civil war.
Beijing views Taiwan as a renegade province and opposes Guatemala's recognition of it.

"There is a shared understanding by the members of the Security Council that China will not exercise its veto power," Foreign Relations Minister Eduardo Stein told a news conference. He said the Security Council would vote on the resolution on Friday or Saturday.

The minister said Guatemala's ambassadors to the United Nations, United States and Canada met with China's representative to the United Nations in New York on Thursday but made no promises to change relations to Taiwan.
"In no way does this mean a backing off or any detriment to the relations Guatemala has with Taiwan," Stein said.
Taiwan is among the five biggest foreign investors in Guatemala, investing mainly in textile-assembly plants, retail businesses and electricity generation, according to Guatemala's Economy Ministry.
Taiwan has targeted several other poor Central American countries for aid and investment. In turn, Central American countries have been firm backers of moves to secure U.N. membership for Taiwan.

Earlier on Thursday, Beijing said Guatemala's ties with Taiwan had destroyed any chance for Beijing's cooperation in the United Nations. But Stein said Guatemala had made gestures to China that it was willing to work for wider relations.
"Guatemala could begin exploratory relations with the Chinese government that could mean an opening in the future," Stein said.

More than 100,000 people died in Guatemala's civil war, the last in Central America, and a further 40,000 "disappeared." Unarmed U.N. military observers would be used to verify a cease-fire and the disarmament of rebels under the terms of Guatemala's Dec. 29 peace accord, hammered out during five years of U.N.-brokered negotiations.
